articles.title: Se filtra la alternativa de Xiaomi al iPhone Ultra: el Xiaomi 18 Fold va a ser una bestia y su diseño lo confirma
articles.text:
El próximo 9 de septiembre, Apple presentará oficialmente su primer móvil plegable: el iPhone Ultra. Este contará con especificaciones nunca vistas en ningún otro dispositivo de esta categoría, y hará que la compañía de Cupertino tenga, por fin, un firme competidor frente a marcas como Samsung, Oppo o Xiaomi. Esta última compañía, eso sí, tiene un as bajo la manga para hacer frente al iPhone Ultra: se llama Xiaomi 18 Fold.
El próximo plegable de Xiaomi se ha dejado ver en nuevas imágenes filtradas, revelando por completo cómo será su diseño y un nuevo color que, curiosamente, también plantará cara a los próximos iPhone 18 Pro. En concreto, el dispositivo contará con un formato "tipo pasaporte". Es decir, tendrá un aspecto mucho más cuadrado cuando está completamente plegado, aunque desplegado cambiará su formato a algo más alargado.
En las imágenes del Xiaomi 18 Fold, podemos ver una parte posterior de una especie de color cereza: un tono que la compañía ya ha utilizado para otros de sus dispositivos. Destaca, además, el módulo fotográfico, que está ubicado de forma horizontal y parece incluir un total de tres sensores: uno más que el iPhone Ultra.
Así son las pantallas del Xiaomi 18 Fold
Otra de las imágenes filtradas muestra parte de la pantalla del Xiaomi 18 Fold con un detalle un tanto curioso: los marcos son mucho más delgados en la parte frontal, que en la parte posterior. Se desconoce si es una estrategia de diseño (por ejemplo, para incluir una batería de mayor tamaño), porque el dispositivo incorpora una funda o porque se trata de un prototipo.
En cualquier caso, la pantalla interior flexible del Xiaomi 18 Fold también se ha dejado ver en un vídeo. Esta, reiteramos, tiene un formato más alargado y llama la atención sus esquinas muy curvadas.
Respecto a las especificaciones, solo sabemos que este Xiaomi 18 Fold será el primer móvil de la marca en incluir el procesador XRING O3 de desarrollo propio. Lamentablemente, es pronto para conocer el resto de características o incluso su fecha de lanzamiento, aunque es probable que llegue antes de que termine el año.

articles.title: US gov't moves to suppress pushback on data centers by removing requirements for public input on pollution — EPA change would allow air pollution permits without publicizing them
articles.text:
US gov't moves to suppress pushback on data centers by removing requirements for public input on pollution — EPA change would allow air pollution permits without publicizing them
States would then need to choose if they want to solicit public feedback for permits.
The U.S. government is looking to move a critical transparency step in the approval of data centers behind closed doors. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has plans to remove a requirement that forces states to seek public feedback on applications for air pollution permits, as reported by The New York Times. The change, if it goes into effect, would apply to a subset of air pollution permits. However, the primary concern is around data centers, as local communities seek to delay, or outright ban, AI data center construction.
The latest proposal applies to permits for a "minor source" of air pollution, which includes landfills, laundromats, steel mills, and, of course, data centers. However, recent analysis of the expansion of AI data centers suggests that environmental impact is growing. The Harvard School of Public Health estimated that the Vantage data center in Loudoun County, Virginia, contributed between $53 million and $99 million in annual health damages, the largest estimate for any single facility ever.
In another example, the analysis conducted by researcher Michael Cork directly influenced a proposal in Fluvanna County, Virginia, to expand a fossil fuel plant. The expansion was ultimately denied based on the findings from the analysis that "shaped the public discussion leading up to the... vote."
The proposal from the EPA would remove, or at least create the opportunity for states to remove, the public discussion that shapes these decisions. The EPA's stance has been that these minor sources don't require federal oversight. However, there's a clear gap when a federal agency decides to stop enforcing federal rules and asks states to step in to make their own decisions.
The Attorneys General from 14 states and three cities signed an open letter opposing the change, writing, "despite the name, even 'minor' sources can pose significant health and environmental impacts." The letter suggests that removing the required publicization of permit applications and 30-day comment period "sidelines these fundamental transparency and democratic safeguards in the name of administrative expediency and relieving regulatory burdens, particularly for accelerating the buildout of data centers and other artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure."
Although the EPA requires a public comment period after an air pollution permit application, the process has been circumvented in some cases.
In Gilroy, California, an Amazon data center began construction last month without the knowledge of many residents. A years-long approval process between the city and Amazon meant the public comment period had lapsed two years before construction began, leaving the public little time to react. In another case, residents of Festus, Missouri sued the city, arguing that it didn't give the public enough time to review a data center proposal before moving forward with it.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
With the EPA's proposed change, responsibility for regulating data centers is placed on the states. Current environmental law allows states to impose stricter environmental standards than the federal minimum, provided the state does not fall below it. The EPA change would allow a state to eliminate the public comment period, since it's not required by federal law.
Currently, a public comment period is still required. The proposed change would go into effect within the next year.

articles.title: Xiaomi’s new Redmi phone lasts for three days on a single charge
articles.text:
The 9,210mAh dual-cell battery in the new Redmi Note 17 Pro Max is the biggest that Xiaomi has fit in any phone it’s sold in Europe — and remarkably, in some other markets the phone comes with an even larger 10,000mAh single-cell design.
Xiaomi’s new Redmi phone lasts for three days on a single charge
The 9,210mAh silicon-carbon battery fits into a phone that’s thinner and lighter than an iPhone 17 Pro Max.
As you can probably guess, this is a silicon-carbon battery either way, one with a high 16 percent silicon content, meaning it’s more energy-dense than most. It’s allowed Xiaomi to fit this huge battery into a phone that’s basically the same size as an iPhone 17 Pro Max, but 8g lighter and fractionally thinner too.
Xiaomi says the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max should give you “worry-free use” for up to three days, or up to 37 hours of continuous video playback. I haven’t been able to put the phone’s battery to the test just yet, but based on the battery life I’ve seen on other recent Android phones, I believe it.
Silicon-carbon cells come with some longevity worries, but the company says this battery should retain 80 percent of its capacity over 1600 charging cycles, which it estimates to be around six years of use. The 100W wired charging should take just over an hour to top the phone up to full, or 20 minutes to get about a day’s worth of power.
Elsewhere, the specs are a mixed bag: a basic Snapdragon 6 Gen 5 chipset, up to 12GB of RAM and 256GB storage, a 6.83-inch OLED display protected by Gorilla Glass Victus 2, and an IP69K rating. As with many Redmi phones, the cameras are the main compromise: a 50-megapixel main with a relatively small sensor, plus an 8-megapixel ultrawide and 32-megapixel selfie camera.
The Note 17 Pro Max is going on sale in Europe, Australia, Latin America, and other global markets, though not the US, at the local equivalent of $499. It’s the top handset in a series of four new Redmi Note 17 models. They share big batteries in common: even the $249, 4G-only Note 17 has a 7,700mAh capacity, which it combines with a mammoth 6.99-inch OLED screen and IP65 protection.

articles.title: Are employees to blame for rise in insider access threats? This new study claims so
articles.text:
Are employees to blame for rise in insider access threats? This new study claims so
Every day, someone is selling access on the dark web
- Flashpoint found ~34 insider threat posts daily on dark web between July 2025–26
- July 2026 saw 12,653 posts, with 75% from insiders selling access themselves
- Report warns insiders are now the weakest link, urging external monitoring of illicit forums
Every month, hundreds of people try to sell access to their employer’s IT infrastructure on the dark web. Some do it for the money. Others do it because they’re angry with their company for whatever reason.
As a result, malicious insiders are growing into one of the biggest, most dangerous threats for modern businesses, experts have warned.
This is according to cybersecurity professionals Flashpoint which published its latest monthly analysis of insider threat recruitment, illicit access advertising, and threat actor activity targeting enterprise environments.
Employees selling, hackers buying
As per the report, between July 2025 and July 2026, there were an average of 34 unique posts on the dark web, every day, which can be classified as “insider threat posts”.
That is roughly a thousand unique posts every month. In July this year alone, Flashpoint analysts identified a total of 12,653 insider posts, including both threat actors attempting to recruit insiders in target organizations, and insiders advertising their services. Of these communications, 1,132 were unique posts.
“As perimeter security, EDR coverage, and other security tools mature, threat actors are finding it faster—and cheaper—to target the human element and simply buy an insider’s credentials or pay an employee to open the front door,” Flashpoint said. “In a threat landscape where identity is becoming the primary attack surface, monitoring illicit marketplaces and recruitment efforts is critical.”
Perhaps the best example is the 2025 Coinbase attack, when hackers bribed overseas customer support employees to provide access to customer data. Coinbase said at the time that the insiders abused legitimate system access, causing a cyber-incident that ended up costing the company around $360 million.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Over the course of the year, the biggest targets were organizations in three industries: telecommunications, retail, and finance. However, July 2026 findings “noticeably deviate from this trend”, Flashpoint said, finding that more than half (58.6%) of all posts affect other industries.
The researchers were still hedging, though, saying that this could also just be a way for threat actors to find an alternative entry point into the target network. Preparations for a supply-chain attack, essentially.
This communication goes both ways, Flashpoint noted. Sometimes it is the criminals offering money for passwords/access, and sometimes it is the insiders advertising their services to the wider cybercriminal community. However, the scales are heavily tilted towards the latter. Just in July this year, more than three quarters (75%) of all unique threat actor posts came from insiders.
“This indicates a highly motivated internal threat landscape where disgruntled employees actively seek out buyers for corporate data and network entry points,” Flashpoint concluded.
Changing the behavior
This report can be both good news, and bad news, depending on the context. It means that software has gotten so good that cybercriminals are moving away from “cracking” it and towards targeting employees who are now the weakest link in the cybersecurity chain.
The bad news is that organizations need to rethink how they defend their perimeter and that they have quite a difficult task at hand:
“Insider threats are inherently difficult to detect using internal security controls alone because the malicious activity relies on valid credentials and legitimate access privileges,” Flashpoint explains. “Relying solely on internal logs means security teams often only detect an insider threat after data exfiltration or system sabotage has already occurred.”
Instead, organizations should monitor deep and dark web forums, invite-only threat communities, as well as encrypted chat platforms, to spot when someone is trying to buy or sell access to their IT infrastructure. They should also keep an eye on infostealer activity, compromised corporate credentials, as well as active session tokens, and make sure they are not used against them.
Finally, they should deploy third-party cybersecurity intelligence that equips teams with adversary TTPs.

articles.title: From Spec To Formal Properties
articles.text:
Can LLMs turn a specification into a set of formal properties that can be used to verify an implementation? The answer is getting closer to being yes, but with caveats.
Key Takeaways:
One of the biggest problems for formal verification has always been the difficulty associated with writing properties. While language standards have been in place for a couple of decades and tools have improved dramatically, that roadblock has never been cleared — perhaps until now, thanks to AI.
AI is known for its ability to read a natural language document and synthesize information from it. One application with high utility would be the ability to read a specification and to automatically create a set of properties that could be used to verify if an implementation matches the specification.
However, several challenges exist, and a number of pitfalls await those who do not fully understand the hazards.
One portion of the SystemVerilog language enables properties of a design to be formally defined. When these properties are used within a verification environment, they are referred to as assertions. Properties define logical and temporal relationships between signals, enabling protocols and other things to be explicitly defined. A set of properties should be able to define the complete set of behaviors intended in a design and to do that without being entangled with how those behaviors are realized. In that respect, they represent a specification against which an RTL implementation can be judged for correctness.
But the SystemVerilogAssertion (SVA) language is not easy to learn, especially given that it is declarative in nature, rather than the object-oriented procedural nature of languages used in most parts of the design and verification flow. For many years, the industry has attempted to create tools and methodologies that make their creation simpler. Recently, LLM-based tools have started to make significant headway even though there are several breakthroughs that still need to be made.
One recent breakthrough is the creation of knowledge graphs, which are defined by Cohen and Chibani [1]. “A knowledge graph stores information as a network of things and the relationships between them, rather than as flat text. It has three parts: nodes (the entities — a signal, a module, a requirement, a port); edges (the relationships — drives, resets, responds-to, belongs-to); and triples, the storage unit, written as (subject → relationship → object).”
KGs act as a database of information that can be quickly accessed, rather than relying on the LLM to extract it every time it’s needed. “Ordinary RAG retrieves chunks of text that look relevant; a KG retrieves specific facts and their connections. That is why the KG-based frameworks argue they give better grounding — there is less chance the model invents a signal name or misreads a relationship, because the relationships are stored explicitly. [1]”
Ironically, one big problem is finding an adequate specification. “The ideal is that you have a perfect spec, but that has not existed at least in the last 30 years,” says Ravindra Aneja, director of applications engineering at Synopsys. “The majority of the time there will not be a perfect spec. In fact, you may not have any spec at all. This may depend on whether it is a new design or a derivative design, who is writing it, and which organization. But until AI came along, the notion of having a perfect spec or documentation was not the coolest thing to do in the world. People often start designing before they fill in the spec because they already have some ideas about what they want to do. With the advent of AI, people are paying more attention.”
A significant amount can be accomplished today. “AI can read a spec document, a protocol standard, or even RTL comments and propose a first pass of assertions covering resets, handshakes, one-hot conditions, and obvious safety checks,” says Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “This is possible when the specifications are on standards that do not change frequently. That draft speeds up the tedious part of writing boilerplate SVA.”
The desire to do this has existed for some time. “People claim that reading a specification and converting it into some other tangible artifact is something that AI is well suited to solve,” says Abhi Kolpekwa, senior vice-president and general manager at Siemens EDA. “It also needs an aspect of change management, because the spec is likely to change. For a verification flow to have change management, there is a lot more that needs to happen outside of agents. This is called contextual intelligence. We need the ability to create a context and contextual intelligence that not only understands the changes, but also makes more informed decisions considering the history and a possible future in the given verification flow context.”
Specifications are never fixed. “I’m in the process of figuring out the spec and I’m doing the development, but marketing then wants this additional feature, and you go back and modify the spec,” says Synopsys’ Aneja. “Sometimes that deviation could be minor. Sometimes it could be major. Whatever changes you are making, how would it reflect in your design and in your verification environment? AI is pretty good at this, figuring out what the deviation is and how it is going to impact your verification. There’s a lot of discussion in the industry about how you can manage this change-based design process. This is where AI is going to be very useful.”
Danger ahead
Was that specification complete? “Completeness is a different question entirely,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “Most real-life silicon development does not happen in isolation. And even when projects are entirely new, it is rare that complete specifications would be written capturing all micro-architecture and architecture, including interfaces where typically most bugs reside. In my experience, AI-generated property sets are strong on structural and syntactic coverage and weak on architectural intent, and the ‘why’ behind a rule. So usefulness is real, but completeness has to be established independently, usually by an engineer who understands the design intent well enough to know what is missing.”
Was all information used? “How useful and complete those assertions are depends on how good your AI engine is, and how accurately it understands the nuances of the specifications,” says Yaron Ilani, design verification solutions engineer at Normal Computing. “At Normal, we tackle this challenge by running ‘auto formalization’ and generating an ontology. The risks could be wrong assumptions resulting from gaps or ambiguity in the specifications. These risks could be mitigated by running a preliminary step of spec auditing.”
Both problems can result in an incomplete set of properties. “The biggest danger is false confidence,” says Darbari. “A team gets a large batch of properties, runs them through a formal tool, sees green proofs, and treats that as sign-off. But a proof is only as good as the property, and a weak or vacuous property proves trivially without checking anything meaningful. AI-generated properties are particularly prone to this because a model can produce syntactically valid SVA that is logically too permissive, missing or over-constraining an antecedent, or checking the wrong signal relationship — and it will still compile and pass.”
That ends up being a verification task itself. “Deriving properties from a spec requires distilling unstructured and multimodal information into provable statements,” says Hanna Yip, product manager lead at Normal. “While the extraction process itself can be efficient, it can be quite challenging to ensure what’s extracted is correct.”
In the past, verification happened when the design team interpreted the specification, the verification team interpreted the specification, and then those interpretations were verified against each other. Sometimes that identified a problem with the specification itself. “Generated properties can quietly encode the AI’s own misreading of the spec as if it were ground truth,” says Darbari. “Errors in interpretation get baked into what looks like a rigorous artifact. There is also a scale risk. If these properties feed downstream FMEDA, safety cases, or certification evidence for ISO 26262 or ISO 21434, an unnoticed gap does not stay contained to one project.”
It quietly means that you cannot trust what AI has done. “Trust is a big issue,” says Kaye Mao, product design lead at Normal. “How do you verify work that you did not do, especially when agents are hyper-confident in their correctness and trained to pass the sniff test? For example, how do you verify a test is actually testing the design as outlined in the spec? Do you have to look at the actual waveforms? That itself is time-consuming, so it may require novel ways of checking agent work.”
Given recent incidents with AI going rogue, Mao adds another potential concern. “Another danger is failing to limit what collateral the agent can access for a given task. Agents will always cheat if possible. For example, they may use the design to generate test cases, which defeats the point of keeping verification and design separate.”
ROI
While it is clear that AI is capable of doing some aspects of the task, it also has costs and creates new work. Does it add up to a significant gain? “I’m increasingly noticing that silicon design houses — even the ones who are building AI hardware powering the agents — are getting nervous about unreasonable use of agentic AI in particular by junior engineers and people who are quick to claim they are experts without the hands-on experience,” says Darbari. “It is efficient at the front end, but it can be inefficient at the back end if teams are not careful.”
This may improve over time. “It depends on how big the spec is,” says Normal’s Kao. “More philosophically, if we define efficiency as saving engineers time, it’s unclear, given the new tasks of verifying agent output, how much actual engineering-time efficiency we see today. I expect efficiency gains to improve as models get better and we devise better ways of verifying agent work.”
There are several ways this can be measured. “Complexity scaling is not strictly computational,” says Arvind Srinivasan, head of solution architect at Normal. “There’s a human efficiency associated with data completeness and review. As with handwritten properties, simple, well-documented parts of a spec are easier to cover than more sophisticated parts of the design. To enable sublinear scaling of formal coverage in modern designs, there is a need to augment existing formal tooling with AI-native formal tooling and alternative, non-SVA autoformalization strategies.”
Scaling has always been an important aspect when formal solvers are used. “There are a lot of techniques in the formal world, which helps you scale,” says Aneja. “The good news is that in the past we had to train junior engineers about these techniques. Now you can provide that knowledge base within these agents, and when they write the property, they can become very efficient in writing those formal properties. That will give you better answers, much faster answers. You’ll be able to do more in the same amount of time. It helps you in scalability.”
Human in the loop
All agentic flows need a human in the loop today. “Drafting hundreds of candidate properties that used to take days of manual reading now takes minutes, and that is a genuine productivity gain,” says Darbari. “Where the efficiency can evaporate is in review. If every generated property or debug waveform needs the same depth of scrutiny as a manually generated one, and the volume has gone up tenfold, the review burden can outpace the drafting savings.”
Someone has to review it. “You can’t just take it as it is because otherwise you’ll be shooting yourself in the foot,” says Aneja. “LLMs can do a lot of interesting stuff, but they can also fool you. That’s the reality of life. It can give you a lot of automation, provide a lot of efficiency and productivity, but someone who knows that design will have to review it manually, tweak it, guide it, and you keep accumulating that information. Over time, you may be able to train it or get to a point where it can do a pretty reasonable job out of the box.”
There are many ways that LLMs can fool you. “Vacuity checking, coverage analysis, and cross-checking against the spec still have to happen, and those steps do not get faster just because generation did,” says Darbari. “They should run vacuity and coverage checks as standard practice, not as an afterthought, because generated sets are more likely to contain trivially true properties than carefully hand-crafted ones.”
But this still creates a problem. “People want to stay in control, because they’re held accountable for the consequences,” says Mao. “It seems unrealistic to expect folks to understand formal. Rather, what other representations can be used to verify the accuracy of a formal representation of a spec? Is it waveforms? Is it something else?”
Standard practices need to be built into the flow. “Treat AI-generated properties as a draft, never as an accepted deliverable,” recommends Darbari. “Build a review gate into the flow before anything reaches a regression suite. Users should insist on provenance — which spec section, which requirement, or which RTL construct produced each property — so reviewers can trace back and check the mapping.”
If trust is built, the gains get larger. “This is good news for DV engineers looking to get into formal verification or assertion-based simulation,” says Normal’s Ilani. “For many years, we used to joke that writing effective formal properties requires a PhD. Now, AI-driven flows lower the barrier to entry for DV engineers looking to run formal verification. Part of this new methodology, in my opinion, is to leverage agentic flows and make them your wingman, your PhD in formal verification assistant, to help you not only understand your formal testbench, but also run it, debug failures, and propose solutions.”
Reference
1. RAG-SVA in the Landscape of LLM-Based Assertion Generation, Cohen and Chibani
[Editor’s Note. Part two will dig deeper into the team skills required and the best ways to introduce those into a methodology. It will explore whether this will enable raising the level of abstraction.]

articles.title: Was weiß die Schufa noch über dich? Jetzt droht ein Streit um alte Daten
articles.text:
Schufa: Datenschützer gehen gegen „Schattendatenbank“ vor – was das bedeutet
Der Auskunftei Schufa droht eine Sammelklage wegen ihrer sogenannten „Schattendatenbank“. Recherchen von NDR und Süddeutscher Zeitung hatten im Juli die Existenz dieser Datenbank öffentlich gemacht. Dort werden “historische Daten“ über teils weit zurückliegende Zahlungsvorgänge von Millionen von Menschen bis zu zehn Jahre gespeichert.
Nun kündigte die österreichische Datenschutzorganisation Noyb (kurz für: „none of your business„) eine Sammelklage gegen die Auskunftei an.
Schufa speichert alte Finanzdaten
Noyb sieht einen klaren Verstoß gegen die Datenschutzgrundverordnung (DSGVO), weil die Schufa die Daten zu lange speichert. Außerdem gibt die Schufa auch bei einem formellen Auskunftsersuchen, das jeder bei ihr stellen kann, bislang keine Auskunft über die Existenz der historischen Daten.
Zwar nutzt die Schufa die veralteten Daten nicht für die Berechnung des aktuellen Scores. Allerdings hebt sie Informationen zu alten Krediten, Pfändungen oder Privatinsolvenzen laut Noyb länger auf, als in der eigenen Datenschutzerklärung angegeben. Demnach werden bezahlte Schulden und Kredite eigentlich nach drei Jahren gelöscht. Tatsächlich werden die Daten aber weiterhin verarbeitet und für „Score-Validierungen“ bei externen Unternehmen genutzt.
Im ersten Schritt fordert Noyb nun von der Schufa, diese Praxis zu unterlassen. In einem zweiten Schritt will die Organisation auch Schadensersatz für die Betroffenen fordern. Bis zum 9. September soll die Auskunftei eine entsprechende Unterlassungserklärung unterschreiben und die Speicherung der alten Daten einstellen. Die Schufa hat aber bereits angekündigt, das nicht zu tun und im Zweifel einen Rechtsstreit bis zum Bundesgerichtshof (BGH) zu führen.
Mit der Verarbeitung der historischen Daten sieht sich die Auskunftei im Recht. Die Daten dienten etwa der Weiterentwicklung von Produkten und Dienstleistungen. Außerdem nutzt die Schufa die alten Daten nach eigenen Angaben, um neue Verfahren zur Risikoberechnung zu testen und zu überprüfen. Die Vergleichstests fänden dabei ausschließlich bei der Schufa statt, Datendetails gehen also nicht an die Auftraggeber.
Warum die Schufa für Verbraucher so wichtig ist
Die Schufa ist die größte Auskunftei in Deutschland. Nach eigenen Angaben hat sie Daten von 68 Millionen Menschen. Daher führt kaum ein Weg an ihr vorbei, wenn man einen Kredit beantragt, einen Mobilfunkvertrag abschließt oder sich um eine Mietwohnung bewirbt.
Wie die Schufa zu ihren Bonitätscores gelangt, war jedoch lange eine Blackbox und Gegenstand von Gerichtsverfahren. Verbraucher:innen beschwerten sich etwa über schlechte Bewertungen, die sie sich nicht erklären konnten oder die auf falschen Daten beruhen.
Zuletzt hatte die Schufa daher eine Transparenzoffensive gestartet und einen neuen Score eingeführt, der auf 12 klar definierten Kriterien beruht, statt wie zuvor rund 250 Einzelmerkmale heranzuziehen.
Wer hinter Noyb steckt
Zu den Gründern des österreichischen Vereins Noyb gehört der Jurist und Aktivist Max Schrems. Er brachte unter anderem das Datenabkommen Privacy Shield zwischen der EU und den USA vor dem Europäischen Gerichtshof (EuGH) zu Fall und erreichte Strafen in Milliardenhöhe gegen BigTech-Firmen wie Google und Meta. Noyb kann als „qualifizierte Einrichtung“ in allen EU-Ländern auch im kollektiven Verbraucherinteresse klagen. Kommt es zu dieser Verbandsklage, könnte sich Betroffene dieser anschließen und gemeinam Schadensersatz fordern.
Im Fall der Schufa kritisiert der Verein auch die bisherige Untätigkeit der zuständigen Datenschutzbehörde in Hessen. Der Landesdatenschutzbeauftragte prüft nach eigenen Angaben den Fall bereits seit dem Frühjahr vergangenen Jahres, bislang liegt aber noch kein Ergebnis vor.

articles.title: Boston Scientific says cyberattack disrupted operations globally
articles.text:
Medical technology company Boston Scientific has been targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted some of its IT systems, causing operational disruptions globally.
The company detected the incident on August 25 and says in an announcement today that it caused a network outage and "impacted access to certain operating systems and business applications, including the ability to process and ship customer orders."
After identifying the intrusion, Boston Scientific activated its incident response procedures and contracted external cybersecurity experts to investigate the impact and help with containment efforts.
The company said it does not yet know when all affected systems will be restored.
“The incident has caused, and is expected to continue to cause, disruptions and limitations of access to certain of the Company’s information systems and business applications that support aspects of the Company’s operations, including the ability to process and ship customer orders,” Boston Scientific states.
“While the Company is working diligently to restore affected functions and systems access, the timeline for a full restoration is not yet known.”
Boston Scientific is a Massachusetts-based medical technology company that develops and manufactures devices used in minimally invasive procedures, including stents, catheters, pacemakers, defibrillators, endoscopes, and others.
It is one of the largest medical device manufacturers in the world, with 59,000 employees, 13 manufacturing facilities, a presence in 127 countries, and annual revenue of over $20 billion in 2025.
Boston Scientific says that its investigation continues as the company is working to determine the nature, scope, and operational or financial consequences of the cybersecurity incident.
In the filing disclosing the attack to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the company does not share any details about the type of cyberattack, the attacker, the initial access method, or whether any data has been exposed or stolen by the threat actor.
At the time of writing, BleepingComputer could not find any data extortion or ransomware threat actor claiming the Boston Scientific breach.
BleepingComputer has contacted the company for more information, but we are still waiting for a response.

articles.title: How Nigeria’s TechAble is bridging the digital inclusion gap for young people with disabilities - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigeria’s TechAble is a an inclusive digital skills and youth empowerment initiative focused on expanding access to technology, STEM education, and future-ready skills for young people in Africa, particularly those with disabilities and from underserved communities.
Formed in 2024 as an initiative of Deafzion Foundation, a Nigeria-based social impact organisation focused on disability rights, inclusive education, and youth empowerment, TechAble came about in response to growing digital exclusion among young people with disabilities.
Through bootcamps, workshops, and community-based programmes, TechAble equips learners with digital literacy, data and AI fundamentals, problem-solving, leadership, and employability skills, while also advocating for inclusive technology ecosystems in Africa.
We identified a major gap in disability-inclusive tech education. While many digital skills programmes exist, very few are intentionally designed to accommodate learners with disabilities or operate within inclusive learning environments,” Emmanuel Izuchukwu Osita, executive director of the Deafzion Foundation and TechAble lead, told Disrupt Africa.
“TechAble differentiates itself by embedding accessibility, inclusive pedagogy, assistive technologies, and psychosocial support into digital skills training.”
Currently funded through grants, partnerships, donations, and in-kind support, the initiative has already trained over 40 youths with disabilities across Nigeria in digital and AI skills, and secured partnerships with organisations such as LEAP Africa, Dow, Windows on America, and state disability agencies.
“Uptake has been strong and organic. We have recorded high interest from students, parents, schools, and partner organisations. Participation rates are high, with strong retention and engagement, particularly among girls with disabilities,” said Osita.
TechAble currently operates in Nasarawa State, Abuja, and Plateau State.
“We plan to expand across other Nigerian states and into selected African countries through partnerships with schools, NGOs, and development agencies,” Osita said.
“Key challenges include limited funding, accessibility costs, infrastructure constraints in underserved areas, and low awareness around disability-inclusive tech education. However, strong community support, partnerships, and demand have enabled us to overcome early-stage challenges and continue scaling.”

articles.title: Galaxy S27 Ultra : Samsung copie (presque) l’iPhone, et ça changerait tout au dos
articles.text:
Le profil du Galaxy S27 Ultra se dessine, et il ne devrait pas tomber trop loin de la pomme. On vous en parlait hier avec une première fuite provenant d’une source réputée, Ice Universe, voici qu’un autre leaker vétéran, OnLeaks, ajoute sa pierre à l’édifice dans les colonnes de Android Headlines.
Le rendu 3D du futur smartphone est ici beaucoup plus détaillé et permet de mieux se rendre compte des changements. Ce qu’on peut constater à ce stade, c’est que le Galaxy S27 Ultra, pour rappel le plus haut de gamme des Galaxy S, devrait peu ou prou conserver les mêmes règles de design, à l’exception notable de son bloc photo.
En effet, Samsung troquerait son habituel bloc photo « épuré » pour une large plaque horizontale sur toute la longueur. Oui cela ressemblerait peu ou prou à ce qu’on trouve au dos d’un iPhone 17 Pro et du futur iPhone 18 Pro, assurément. Vous constaterez en outre la disparition d’un des modules photo, sans doute le X3, qui n’a plus vraiment lieu d’être avec un capteur principal de 200 Mpx qui peut très bien atteindre une focale équivalente en zoomant numériquement dans le capteur.
OnLeaks confirme en outre des informations précédentes, à savoir que les dimensions seraient peu ou prou les mêmes que celle du Galaxy S26 Ultra, à savoir 163.76 x 78.25 x 7.97 mm très précisément. Le bloc photo amènerait le téléphone à 12,53 mm d’épaisseur.
Quelle fiche technique pour le Galaxy S27 Ultra ?
Pour l’heure, les rumeurs ne sont pas légion, mais on peut d’ores et déjà tabler sur un lancement en début d’année, aux alentours des mois de janvier et février 2027.
Le Galaxy S27 Ultra devrait intégrer la prochaine puce haut de gamme de Qualcomm, le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, un écran de 6,9 pouces ainsi qu’une batterie un peu plus volumineuse cette année, autour des 5700 mAh.

articles.title: The/Nudge launches Rs 250 Cr TILT fund for early-stage impact startups
articles.text:
The/Nudge launches Rs 250 Cr TILT fund for early-stage impact startups
TILT will primarily invest in startups at the seed to Series A stages, with cheque sizes ranging from Rs 2 crore to Rs 16 crore.
The/Nudge Foundation has launched TILT, its first impact investment platform, with a corpus of Rs 250 crore to invest in science and technology-led businesses.
The fund is backed by the Livelihood Impact Fund, along with prominent entrepreneurs and investors such as Deep Kalra (MakeMyTrip), Amit Gupta (Yulu), Hari Menon (BigBasket), Binny Bansal (Flipkart), Vidit Aatrey (Meesho), and the Raj & Indra Nooyi Family Office.
TILT will primarily invest in startups at the seed to Series A stages, with cheque sizes ranging from Rs 2 crore to Rs 16 crore. According to the foundation, the platform aims to address a gap in India’s entrepreneurial ecosystem—the limited availability of patient, impact-focused capital for ventures in their early stages.
TILT will invest across agricultural value chains, climate resilience, informal work, and emerging employment models, MSME productivity, employability, financial inclusion, market access and distribution, and technology and AI applied to livelihood challenges.
The fund will also support areas such as research, market development, partnerships and ecosystem infrastructure, complementing the venture fund’s investment work.
“India’s Next Billion is increasingly ready for scalable market solutions, and our focus is on backing founders early, giving them the time to build resilient models and aligning capital more closely with the realities of the markets and communities they serve,” said Richa Singh, Co-founder and Managing Partner, TILT.
Over the past eight years, The/Nudge has supported livelihood-focused social entrepreneurs, backing more than 190 social enterprises and deploying around Rs 180 crore in grants.
As these ventures moved from early validation to scale, it became clear that many needed more than philanthropic support to realise their full potential, the foundation said. They also required patient, impact-first investment capital to help them navigate the formative stages of building resilient businesses and achieving sustainable scale.
TILT Managing Partner & Founder Atul Satija said, “Over the next 15 years, we aim to back 150+ startups and meaningfully improve 100 million lives. We hope to show what becomes possible when capital is designed around the realities of impact-led businesses.”
Edited by Megha Reddy

articles.title: Un prototype de break aperçu pour la troisième fois près du siège de XPeng
articles.text:
Les nouveautés s’enchaînent chez XPeng. En l’espace de deux mois, le constructeur chinois a dévoilé deux SUV 100 % électriques pour étoffer sa gamme : le Mona L03 en juillet et le G9L ce mois d’août. Et bientôt un troisième modèle d’ici la fin de l’année ? La marque basée à Guangzhou plancherait en tout cas sur un mystérieux modèle, rapporte Electric Vehicles ce 27 août 2026.
Mais cette fois, pas de SUV, il semblerait que nous ayons affaire à un break. Les clichés pris de profil laissent deviner une carrosserie plus proche de ce que l’on appelle « shooting brake » que du break carré traditionnel : le toit reste plat depuis le montant central avant de plonger vers l’arrière, avec une lunette arrière généreuse et un becquet sur le hayon. Le trois-quarts avant montre un nez fermé, sans calandre apparente et des caméras logées dans les rétroviseurs.
Un nom de code et c’est tout
Selon plusieurs sources proches du dossier citées par le média local 21st Century Business Herald, le véhicule porterait la désignation D11T en interne, le « T » faisant référence à « Travel », le voyage donc. Dans la nomenclature de la gamme Mona, les codes existants étaient D01 pour la berline M03, D02 et D03 pour les SUV L05 et L03.
Le break n’a fait l’objet d’aucun dépôt auprès du ministère chinois de l’Industrie et des Technologies de l’information, l’étape administrative qui rend publiques les dimensions, le poids, les fournisseurs de moteurs et la chimie des batteries d’un modèle chinois. À titre de comparaison, XPeng avait déposé en mai les dossiers du G9L et ceux des Mona L05 et L03, pour une officialisation quelques mois plus tard.
Lors de la publication des résultats du deuxième trimestre le 24 août, la direction n’a fait aucune mention du projet. Idem lors du salon de Chengdu, en Chine, qui se tient en ce moment (21-30 août 2026). Une source interne aurait toutefois confirmé au blogueur à l’origine des premières photos espions que le programme de développement était bien concret.
Un segment des breaks qui prend de l’ampleur
XPeng n’est pas seul sur ce terrain. Lynk&Co, Zeekr, Avatr, Denza ou encore Nio, les marques chinoises ont trouvé un regain d’intérêt pour ce type de carrosserie, longtemps délaissée au profit des SUV.
Selon l’association chinoise des constructeurs automobiles (CAAM), le segment des breaks représentait environ 176 000 immatriculations en Chine en 2025, soit moins de 1 % des ventes. D’ici la fin de l’année 2026, cette part devrait grimper à 3 %, soit environ 250 000 exemplaires.

articles.title: Ça se rapproche ! Les robotaxis de Waymo débarquent sur les routes allemandes, sa première dans l'UE
articles.text:
Waymo vient d’annoncer le lancement de ses premiers tests de robotaxis à Munich, avec l’ouverture d’un service commercial dès la fin 2027. Une nouvelle étape qui confirme les ambitions de la filiale de Google en Europe.
Et sa feuille de route est déjà toute tracée. Pour commencer, l’entreprise va cartographier manuellement les rues de la ville bavaroise, avant de faire circuler ses véhicules avec des conducteurs de sécurité à bord puis, une fois la technologie validée, sans personne au volant. Les premiers passagers seront des employés et des invités, avant l’ouverture au grand public.
Un cadre légal déjà présent
« Munich est un pôle mondial de la mobilité et de l'ingénierie, et faire partie de cette ville marque une étape importante de notre expansion mondiale », fait valoir Tekedra Mawakana, co-PDG de Waymo. Car la métropole concentre une bonne partie de l’industrie automobile allemande et plus globalement, nos voisins disposent d’un cadre légal déjà prêt à accueillir ce type de technologie, fait rare sur le Vieux Continent.
Dès 2021, l’Allemagne est en effet devenue le premier pays de l’Union européenne (UE) à se doter d’une législation pour réglementer la conduite autonome de niveau 4, c’est-à-dire capable de gérer l’intégralité de la conduite sans intervention humaine, dans certaines conditions données.
« Le fait qu'une entreprise comme Waymo s'intéresse à l'Allemagne souligne l'attrait de notre marché et prouve que des services de mobilité autonome réguliers peuvent fonctionner chez nous. Nous devons désormais tirer parti des atouts de notre économie et développer des solutions de mobilité autonome au sein même de l'Europe », se félicite Christian Hirte, secrétaire d’État parlementaire au ministère fédéral des Transports.
L’entreprise assure, en outre, que ses véhicules autonomes vont non seulement apporter des solutions de mobilité plus sûres, ils vont également faciliter le quotidien des personnes atteintes de cécité, en levant « certains des obstacles auxquels sont confrontés les utilisateurs de chiens guides d’aveugles lorsqu’ils recourent aux services traditionnels de taxi et de VTC ». Pour ces acteurs, la concurrence s’annonce très rude.
Et la France, alors ?
Car Waymo s’impose comme un poids lourd de la conduite autonome. La société américaine revendique plus de 20 millions de trajets effectués et des centaines de milliers de courses commerciales chaque semaine. S ur sa terre natale, elle opère déjà des services dans 11 villes, et a même décidé de restreindre son partenariat exclusif avec Uber, signe qu’elle n’a plus besoin de s’appuyer sur une plateforme tierce pour croître.
Par ailleurs, Waymo teste déjà ses véhicules à Londres, où un service commercial devrait être proposé d’ici à la fin de l’année. Et la France pourrait être la prochaine. Fin juin, l’entreprise a discrètement fait enregistrer une filiale à Paris afin de « fournir des services de transport à la demande à l'aide de véhicules autonomes ». En revanche, aucun calendrier n’a, pour le moment, été communiqué.

articles.title: Apple Mac Studio M5 Ultra and Mac Mini M6 Launched
articles.text:
Apple introduced two desktops this week, sending M6 into the new Mac mini and M5 Ultra into the new Mac Studio. The Apple M6 is the company’s first 2 nm desktop part and targets the mainstream desktop, while M5 Ultra is a quad-die design with up to 512GB of unified memory for high-capacity local AI and professional compute. Apple published the full announcement alongside the launch. We are a bit behind, just given our massive Hot Chips 2026 coverage.
Apple M6 and M5 Ultra
The Apple M6 brings a 12-core CPU split into two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores, joined by a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. Unified memory tops out at 32GB with up to 170GB/s of bandwidth. Apple claims 1.2x faster multithreaded CPU performance than M5, nearly 30 percent more peak GPU AI compute, and 10 percent more memory bandwidth. Apple also says the Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers up to 2x peak compute over prior generations and that both engines can run at once for faster model execution. We called the Apple Mac Mini M4 the standard for compact desktops in earlier coverage, and this refresh carries that mini form factor forward.
The M5 Ultra is the larger of the pair. Apple UltraFusion ties two dual-die M5 Max chips into one quad-die SoC, with an inter-die fabric Apple rates above 4.4TB/s. Scaling reaches a 36-core CPU with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, an 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a 32-core Neural Engine. Unified memory still supports up to 512GB but is served by 1.2TB/s of bandwidth, which Apple says is 50 percent higher than the M3 Ultra. Apple claims up to 1.3x faster multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra, again from preproduction parts. Another fun note is that the M5 Ultra has a PCIe Gen6 SSD, which is faster than the M.2 SSDs currently on the market.
We called the prior M3 Ultra Mac Studio the big local AI play. That capacity holds large language models that common discrete GPUs cannot fit, and the faster 1.2TB/s pool should improve tokens-per-second for on-device inference. Higher bandwidth and an updated GPU hopefully mean that this is notably better. We are focused on the M5 Ultra, but there is an M5 Max version as well with up to an 18-core CPU, 40-core GPU, and 128GB of memory.
Final Words
Pricing has certainly increased. An Apple Mac Studio M3 Ultra 512GB we purchased for around $10K, but the 256GB M5 Ultra model is over $11K. Apple says the new M5 Ultra 512GB will be available in October, so for now you can only order the 256GB model. It will be interesting to see how much that one costs.
Something worth considering is that, from a desk-side AI perspective, the NVIDIA GB300 Station line is about $100K but offers an NVIDIA GPU with several times higher memory bandwidth and more total system memory. We had a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 Fast model running at well over 26K tokens/s at c=512, which is wild to see.
Local AI is getting really cool.

articles.title: Recent Citrix NetScaler Vulnerability Exploited in the Wild
articles.text:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is urging government organizations to immediately address a recently patched Citrix NetScaler vulnerability that is being exploited in the wild.
The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-8452 and it was one of the several flaws for which Citrix announced patches on June 30.
The vendor said the vulnerability can only be exploited against appliances configured as an AAA virtual server or a Gateway VPN server. Versions 14.1-72.61 (FIPS), 13.1-63.18 and 13.1-37.272 fix the security hole.
Citrix’s advisory for CVE-2026-8452 describes it as a high-severity memory overflow that can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior and DoS attacks.
However, cybersecurity firm WatchTowr has analyzed the vulnerability and demonstrated that it can be exploited for unauthenticated remote code execution. WatchTowr made details and PoC code public on August 14.
Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) and Defused started seeing in-the-wild exploitation shortly after. The former reported that the attackers had been dropping a web shell and executing discovery commands such as ‘id’ and ‘echo’.
CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on August 26 and instructed agencies to address it by August 29.
The advisory from Citrix has yet to be updated to confirm in-the-wild exploitation.
This is the second vulnerability exploited in recent months, after the CitrixBleed-like NetScaler vulnerability CVE-2026-8451, which threat actors started exploiting within 24 hours of its public disclosure.

articles.title: « Les caméras ne suffisent pas » : Google descend Tesla… sans jamais prononcer son nom
articles.text:
Le 26 août, Srikanth Thirumalai, vice-président du logiciel embarqué de Waymo, a publié un billet listant dix enseignements tirés de plus de 200 millions de miles parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, soit plus de 320 millions de kilomètres.
Le texte ne cite jamais Tesla. Pourtant, à peu près tout le secteur y a lu une charge contre l’approche de Musk, et Axios, à qui Thirumalai a accordé un entretien, y voit une attaque directe visant Tesla. Le calendrier n’aide pas à croire au hasard : le Cybercab de Tesla est lancé la semaine prochaine.
Les caméras seules suffisent-elles ? Waymo répond clairement non
C’est le tout premier enseignement du billet, et le plus polémique. Waymo l’écrit noir sur blanc : « les caméras sont formidables, mais elles ne suffisent pas ». De fait, son véhicule empile les capteurs : 13 caméras, 4 LiDAR (des lasers qui mesurent les distances en 3D), 6 radars et des microphones. Chacun couvre les angles morts des autres.
Le LiDAR dessine le relief au millimètre, la caméra lit les panneaux et la couleur des feux, le radar « voit » à travers la pluie, le brouillard ou la poussière. En face, Tesla mise sur les caméras seules, sans LiDAR ni radar, comme le rappelle InsideEVs. L’argument de Thirumalai tient en une phrase : l’IA ne peut interpréter que ce qu’elle perçoit, et si le capteur ne voit rien, le logiciel ne peut pas faire grand-chose.
Cartes HD et « boîte noire » : l’autre grande dispute
Le deuxième point de friction porte sur les cartes haute définition. Waymo cartographie chaque zone à l’avance et s’en sert comme d’une mémoire, un repère fiable quand la visibilité est mauvaise. Tesla juge cette étape inutile et préfère un système qui apprend tout seul.
C’est là qu’intervient le troisième désaccord, sans doute le plus technique : l’architecture « end-to-end » (de bout-en-bout) pure. En clair, un seul réseau de neurones qui prend les pixels bruts des caméras et sort directement les commandes de direction, sans modules intermédiaires.
Waymo prévient que ce genre de système fonctionne comme une boîte noire dont on comprend mal les décisions. Interrogé par Axios, Thirumalai résume : les systèmes purement end-to-end n’atteignent pas son niveau de sécurité à l’échelle où Waymo opère, et il n’existe selon lui « pas de raccourci » par l’IA. C’est justement la méthode utilisée par Tesla.
    Pour aller plus loin
            « On ne sent pas que c’est un robot qui conduit » : j’ai testé Zoox, l’étonnant robot-taxi sans volant d’Amazon
            
Pour autant, le débat est loin d’être tranché. Tesla n’est pas seul à défendre l’approche adverse : des acteurs comme Wayve ou Waabi parient eux aussi sur ces réseaux « bout en bout », qu’ils présentent comme la voie la plus rapide vers une IA capable de raisonner comme un humain.
Waymo, de son côté, a testé ces outils avant de conclure qu’ils manquaient de garde-fous. Chaque camp roule donc avec sa conviction, et personne n’a encore la preuve définitive que l’autre a tort. D’ailleurs, les batailles de chiffres de sécurité font rage : entre ceux de Waymo et ceux publiés par Tesla.
500 000 trajets par semaine contre un lancement très attendu
Sur le terrain, l’écart est net. Waymo revendique plus de 500 000 trajets payants par semaine dans une quinzaine de villes américaines, sans conducteur de sécurité à bord. Tesla, lui, prépare encore son grand rendez-vous : le Cybercab est lancé le 3 septembre à Austin, un véhicule à deux places sans volant ni pédales.
Le service Tesla d’Austin tourne pour l’instant avec une quarantaine de voitures, et la plupart des courses embarquent toujours un opérateur humain sur le siège avant, alors qu’Elon Musk promettait de les retirer fin 2025.
Un point de prudence sur ce rendez-vous du 3 septembre : c’est un événement de lancement sur invitation, retransmis en direct, pas une mise en circulation massive ni un feu vert réglementaire. Le Cybercab vise la flotte de robotaxis, pas la vente aux particuliers, et Tesla ne prendra pas de commandes ce jour-là. La version de série sera montrée, mais le déploiement à grande échelle reste encore à mettre en place.
Le LiDAR recule partout, sauf chez ceux qui y croient
Le duel dépasse le seul face-à-face Waymo–Tesla. Chez les constructeurs, le LiDAR recule sur plusieurs fronts. Tesla n’en veut pas, et le chinois Xpeng a fait le même pari du tout-caméra, y compris sur ses voitures vendues en France.
Volvo a retiré le LiDAR de ses EX90 et ES90, mais pas par conviction : son fournisseur Luminar a fait faillite, et le constructeur a même dû dédommager ses premiers clients. À l’inverse, l’équipementier français Valeo continue de miser gros sur le capteur laser.
Au fond, l’enjeu est autant industriel que technique. Les cartes HD imposent de cartographier chaque zone avant d’y rouler, une contrainte de déploiement lourde. Le LiDAR, lui, coûte cher, ce qui explique pourquoi certains le jugent voué à disparaître. La question divise : les LiDAR pourraient disparaître de certaines voitures quand d’autres parient au contraire sur leur démocratisation. Si vous vous demandez encore à quoi ils servent vraiment, tout part de là : voir mieux, ou apprendre à se passer de mieux voir.
Pour le lecteur français, l’affrontement reste lointain, mais il se rapproche : Google a monté une filiale française pour Waymo (disponible en Grande-Bretagne et en Allemagne), même s’il faudra encore patienter avant de commander un robotaxi à Paris. En parallèle, le FSD de Tesla poursuit son arrivée en Europe.
Sur le papier, Waymo a des arguments solides : des années d’avance, un service commercial qui tourne sans chauffeur et des volumes que Tesla n’égale pas encore. Son billet ne clôt pas le débat pour autant, puisque les progrès de l’IA pourraient un jour donner raison aux partisans du tout-caméra. Le 3 septembre, le Cybercab apportera un premier élément de réponse concret.

articles.title: En Aste Nagusia ya llevan 14 detenidos y casi 150 kilos de comida requisada y tirada a la basura
articles.text:
Dos agentes heridos y uno de ellos tuvo que abandonar el servicio. Lo confirmaba este miércoles la Policía Municipal de Bilbao, resumiendo la cuarta jornada de la Aste Nagusia 2026. El balance actual de la festividad más importante de la ciudad: 14 detenidos, dos por tocamientos (violencia machista), 64 denuncias, 50 de ellas por hurto. Un día antes, el tercero de fiesta, la cifra fue de ocho detenciones y 55 kilos de comida no autorizada decomisada en distintos puntos del recinto. La Semana Grande bilbaína, que este año reúne a más de un millón de personas entre el 22 y el 30 de agosto, no solo no acepta pagos en digital, tampoco se libra del trapicheo ilegal.
Una fiesta, dos economías. Bajo el paraguas oficial de la Aste Nagusia conviven dos sistemas de venta de comida y bebida completamente distintos. Uno es el de las txosnas, las casetas gestionadas por Bilboko Konpartsak desde 1978, con licencia, control sanitario y una tradición que financia actividades sociales y culturales. El otro es informal, ambulante y sin ningún permiso. Pero no es lo mismo comprar unas latas del Eroski a 0,60 euros y revenderlas a dos euros que montar una barbacoa improvisada para vender txistorra o paella al peso entre la multitud.
La Policía Municipal tolera de facto la primera práctica. Entre la masa humana del Arenal es complicado detectar este mercadeo. Pero corta de raíz la segunda porque implica manipulación de alimentos sin control sanitario. El martes, sobre las 13:30 horas, varios testigos denunciaron a dos personas que cocinaban una paella en pleno concurso de tortillas y la ofrecían a 3 euros la ración. Los agentes llegaron, confirmaron la venta ilegal y obligaron a los responsables a tirar la paella entera a un contenedor de basura. Espátula en mano, no quedó un gramo de arroz.
Las cifras del desecho. Los números de esta edición superan con holgura los de 2025. Solo entre la noche del domingo y el lunes se requisaron 90 kilos de comida en puestos ilegales. Sumando el decomiso de 55 kilos del martes, la Aste Nagusia de 2026 ya roza en cuatro días los 202 kilos incautados durante las 9 jornadas completas del año pasado. El Ayuntamiento no ha informado si el repunte se debe a más guardias policiales, a más vendedores ambulantes, o a ambas cosas a la vez.
Esto no detiene el trapicheo de comida ilegal, más bien al contrario: mientras la Hacienda foral estrena trazabilidad fiscal completa sobre cada consumición, el dinero fluye igual que hace casi medio siglo: en billetes, de mano en mano, sin dejar rastro.
El año del pago a mano. Ni tarjeta ni Bizum, solo dinero en metálico, con datáfonos para tener tique, pero nada más. Bilboko Konpartsak lo justificó como una tradición de siempre. 2026 es también el primer año en que Euskadi exige facturación electrónica obligatoria mediante el sistema Batuz y el TicketBai, y las txosnas admiten estar todavía "en fase de ensayo" con esos terminales.
Una conversación paralela habla de intereses políticos: históricamente, algunas txosnas fueron vía de financiación del entorno abertzale: la propia Wikipedia sobre ETA recoge que la organización llegó a recaudar fondos en herriko tabernas y en algunas casetas de fiestas populares. La propia Bilboko Konpartsak admitió en 2010 que no podía "garantizar" que parte de la recaudación no terminara en manos de grupos de apoyo a presos de ETA. El propio movimiento GKS reconoció en 2022 que las casetas eran "una fuente de financiación imprescindible" y El Confidencial lo documentó en 2024. En 2025, la Ertzaintza investigó un hallazgo de 5.635 euros en efectivo presuntamente vinculados a financiación proetarra procedente de comparsas, las cuales se resisten alegando que "no son empresas". Ninguna prueba de financiación directa ni judicialmente vinculante, pero hay migas y rastros que conducen a cierta opacidad.
Dónde va a parar lo requisado. ¿Qué pasa con los 145 kilos de comida decomisados en cuatro días? Quienes estamos obsesionados con no tirar nada miramos con pena esa paella y esos guisos que acaban al fondo del contenedor verde o marrón oscuro. Si bien la idea de requisar y regalar (repercutiendo las pérdidas sobre quien busca hacer negocio) es sugerente, los agentes se deshacen de ella delante de todo el mundo.
Esta comida no puede ser donada a un banco de alimentos o redistribuida de otra forma porque carece de un control de trazabilidad que garantice cero intoxicaciones. La comida no vendida no vuelve a ningún plato. Y más de un millón de estómagos se alimentan en la mítica festividad.

articles.title: Bolt and Mombasa County to license 400 delivery riders
articles.text:
Bolt, the Estonian mobility platform, has partnered with the government of Mombasa County, Kenya’s second-largest city, to launch a programme to help 400 delivery riders in the county obtain formal licences.
The programme will use Kenya’s Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) framework, which allows workers who have gained skills through practical experience to have those skills assessed and formally recognised. Enrolled riders will complete 21 days of accredited training through a certified driving school before receiving their licences from Kenya’s National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA), based on their demonstrated competency.
The programme is part of a partnership between Bolt and the Mombasa County government that began with a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2026. Under the agreement, both parties work together to improve compliance and safety in the transport sector, support youth employment and help transport businesses adopt digital platforms.
The partnership comes as Kenya grapples with how to formally recognise and regulate its motorcycle and app-based delivery economy. More than 2 million riders are active in Kenya’s boda-boda sector, according to a 2025 parliamentary report, making it a major source of employment. However, the report noted that many operators remain improperly documented or professionally trained. Bolt and Mombasa County’s programme is an effort to bring riders into the formal transport system by providing experienced delivery workers with a path to recognised training and licensing.
“We are very happy to be partnering with Bolt as we launch this training for our delivery riders,” said HE. Abdulswamad Shariff Nassir, Governor of Mombasa County. “Our partnership with Bolt demonstrates the value of public-private collaboration in delivering practical solutions that improve the lives of our residents. By formally recognising the skills our riders already have, and giving them a clear path to a licence and a livelihood they can be proud of, this programme reflects our vision of a competitive, inclusive and future-ready Mombasa.”
The programme is intended for delivery riders who have practical experience but lack the formal qualification required for licensing. Under the RPL framework, their existing riding skills are assessed against recognised standards.
Bolt has also committed KES 1.5 million ($11,591) to support the partnership with Mombasa County. The investment will support rider and driver compliance, training and licensing, and the digitisation of transport businesses across the county.
The partnership also includes sharing trip and demand data with the county. The data is expected to help the government understand transport patterns and plan infrastructure, including the potential placement of electric-vehicle charging points.
“This is a deliberate policy intervention to correct a long-standing imbalance between the skills thousands of young riders already have and the formal recognition the system has never given them,” said Benjamin Sulle, public policy manager at Bolt. “A licence has to be earned through demonstrated, certified competency, which is why every rider on this programme completes 21 days of accredited training before they are licensed. Once they are, the opportunity extends well beyond food delivery.”
The timing comes as the economics of operating on mobility platforms remain under pressure in Kenya. In May, Bolt raised ride-hailing fares in the country by 6% after rising fuel prices increased drivers’ operating costs. Petrol prices in Nairobi had reached KES 197.60 ($1.53) per litre after Kenya’s April fuel-price review, while ride-hailing drivers had staged protests and threatened strikes in the months preceding the hike.
Against that backdrop, Bolt said its partnership with the county is also aimed at creating a more compliant and sustainable transport ecosystem for riders and local businesses.
“At Bolt, we believe the future of mobility is built through meaningful partnerships. The investment made into the Recognition of Prior Learning is a demonstration of our commitment to supporting Mombasa County’s vision for a modern, safe and technology-enabled transport ecosystem,” said Arthur Gacharia, senior operations manager, Rides, Kenya.
“By working together to promote compliance, empower riders, and help local businesses embrace digital opportunities, we are investing in the long-term growth and resilience of the county’s economy.”
In July, Bolt also integrated its ride-hailing service with ChatGPT, allowing users across Africa and global markets to book rides through OpenAI’s chatbot.

articles.title: “Dévastateur pour nous” : les créateurs de GTA 6 sortent du silence après une semaine de chaos
articles.text:
“Dévastateur pour nous” : les créateurs de GTA 6 sortent du silence après une semaine de chaos
Rockstar Games a publié un communiqué officiel ce 26 août 2026, qualifiant les fuites de gameplay de Grand Theft Auto VI de "dévastatrices", tout en confirmant l'Extended Look prévu demain sur Netflix et la sortie au 19 novembre.
Huit jours de silence, puis trois paragraphes soigneusement pesés. Rockstar Games a fini par répondre à la vague de leaks qui inonde les réseaux depuis le 18 août, orchestrée par le groupe de hackers CyberLeek. Une dizaine d'extraits de gameplay, une carte complète de l'Etat fictif de Leonida et près de 19 minutes de séquences tirées d'un build ancien (estimé entre 2022 et 2023) ont circulé en ligne avant d'être frappés par des rafales de retraits DMCA.
Rockstar s'excuse et confirme l'Extended Look du 27 août
Le ton du communiqué, publié sur leurs réseaux oscille entre contrition et réassurance. Le studio s'excuse pour la durée du développement, glisse que le jeu est "quasiment terminé" et annonce que l'Extended Look sera bien diffusé demain, 27 août, en avant-première sur Netflix à 21 h (heure française), puis sur YouTube six heures plus tard.
— Rockstar Games (@RockstarGames) August 26, 2026
	
Dire que voir des vidéos de gameplay de Grand Theft Auto VI fuiter de cette manière a été dévastateur pour notre équipe serait en dessous de la vérité, et ce n'est évidemment pas ainsi que nous voulions vous montrer le jeu après tout ce temps.
Le studio remercie au passage la communauté pour ses messages de soutien, et confirme que la date de sortie reste fixée au 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S.
Ce que Rockstar ne dit pas sur les fuites de GTA 6
Le communiqué est aussi remarquable par ses silences : aucune mention de CyberLeek, aucun mot sur les poursuites judiciaires, alors que Take-Two Interactive a déjà déposé des subpoenas auprès d'un tribunal fédéral pour identifier les responsables. Rien sur la nature exacte du build compromis ni sur la faille exploitée. Rockstar préfère braquer les projecteurs sur demain, et laisser ses avocats travailler dans l'ombre.
